opening: Guarantees that hold however unlucky you are.

steps.prompt: A drawer holds socks of 3 colours. How many must you take, without looking, to be certain of having two of the same colour?
nudges: What is the worst that can happen with three socks?
steps.showed: Three socks can all be different; a fourth must repeat a colour.

steps.prompt: With 4 colours, how many socks guarantee three of the same colour?
nudges: How many socks can you hold with at most two of each colour?
steps.showed: Two of each colour is 8 socks with no triple; the ninth forces one.

steps.prompt: How many whole numbers must you pick to be certain that two of them leave the same remainder when divided by 7?
nudges: How many different remainders are there?
steps.showed: Seven possible remainders, so eight numbers.

steps.prompt: Six different numbers are chosen from 1 to 10. Must two of them add up to 11?
options: Yes: the pairs (1,10), (2,9), (3,8), (4,7), (5,6) are five boxes for six numbers
nudges: Which numbers add up to 11 with which?
steps.showed: The trick is choosing the boxes: here each box is a pair summing to 11.

steps.prompt: What is the smallest k such that any k different numbers from 1 to 20 include two that differ by exactly 10?
steps.verify:
import itertools
result = next(k for k in range(1, 21) if all(any(abs(x - y) == 10 for x, y in itertools.combinations(c, 2)) for c in itertools.combinations(range(1, 21), k)))
nudges: Which pairs of numbers differ by 10? How many such pairs are there?
steps.showed: Ten boxes (1,11), (2,12), ..., (10,20): one number from each avoids it, an eleventh cannot.

steps.prompt: What is the largest number of different numbers you can choose from 1 to 10 so that none of them divides another?
steps.verify: result = max(bin(m).count('1') for m in range(1 << 10) if not any(m >> i & 1 and m >> j & 1 and (j + 1) % (i + 1) == 0 for i in range(10) for j in range(i + 1, 10)))
nudges: The numbers 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 work. Can six numbers work?
steps.showed: Five, for example 6 to 10. To see that six is impossible you need the right boxes.

steps.prompt: Which boxes show that among any six numbers from 1 to 10 one divides another?
options: Group numbers by their largest odd divisor: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 give five boxes, and within a box each number is a power of two times the next smaller
Group numbers by their last digit
nudges: Write each number as an odd number times a power of two. If two numbers share the odd part, how are they related?
steps.showed: Five odd parts, so five boxes; two numbers in one box differ by a power of two, so one divides the other.

steps.prompt: When a problem says "show that some two of them must ...", what should you look for?
options: A way to sort the objects into fewer boxes than there are objects, such that two in one box have the wanted property
A clever ordering of the objects
nudges: What did the pairs summing to 11 and the odd parts have in common?
steps.showed: The whole difficulty is inventing the boxes.

steps.prompt: Prove that among any $n + 1$ whole numbers there are two whose difference is divisible by $n$.
claims: Every whole number has one of the n remainders 0, 1, ..., n-1 when divided by n.
There are n + 1 numbers and only n possible remainders, so two of the numbers have the same remainder.
Two numbers with the same remainder differ by a multiple of n.
nudges: Why do two numbers in the same box have the wanted property?

steps.prompt: What is the largest number of different numbers you can choose from 1 to 20 so that none of them divides another?
steps.verify:
import functools
@functools.lru_cache(None)
def best(i, chosen):
    if i > 20: return 0
    skip = best(i + 1, chosen)
    return max(skip, 1 + best(i + 1, chosen + (i,))) if all(i % c for c in chosen) else skip
result = best(1, ())
nudges: 11 to 20 is one choice of ten. Which boxes show that eleven is impossible?
steps.showed: Ten boxes, one for each odd number up to 19 (a number goes in the box of its largest odd divisor); two numbers in one box divide each other. So ten is the most, reached by 11..20.

steps.prompt: What is the largest number of different numbers you can choose from 1 to 20 so that no two of them differ by exactly 4 or exactly 7?
steps.verify: result = max(bin(m).count('1') for m in range(1 << 20) if not m & (m >> 4) and not m & (m >> 7))
nudges: Any eleven numbers in a row: can you arrange them in a circle so that neighbours differ by 4 or 7?
How many can you take from such a circle?
steps.showed: Any eleven numbers in a row form a single cycle under "differ by 4 or 7" (for 1..11: 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 10, 3, 7, 11, 4, 8, back to 1), and from a cycle of eleven you can take at most 5. So 1..11 gives at most 5, and 12..20, being part of such a cycle, at most 5 more. Ten is reachable.

steps.prompt: Nine points form a 3 by 3 grid. What is the smallest k such that any k of the points include three on one straight line?
steps.verify:
import itertools
pts = [(x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(3)]
line = lambda a, b, c: (b[0] - a[0]) * (c[1] - a[1]) == (b[1] - a[1]) * (c[0] - a[0])
free = max(len(c) for k in range(10) for c in itertools.combinations(pts, k) if not any(line(*t) for t in itertools.combinations(c, 3)))
result = free + 1
nudges: Each row can contribute at most how many points to a set with no three in line?
steps.showed: Each of the three rows is a line, so at most two points per row: at most six. Six is possible (two per row, chosen to dodge columns and diagonals), so seven forces a line.

reveal.name: Pigeonhole principle
reveal.statement: If more than $kn$ objects are placed in $n$ boxes, some box holds more than $k$ of them. In particular $n + 1$ objects in $n$ boxes force two into one box.
reveal.remark: In problems it usually appears as "there are only so many possible values, so something repeats": remainders, states of a process, prefix sums mod n.
